rationale: A wins because it keeps the story honest: "flies power lines with nobody at the controls — and no named utility willing to say so" is the actual tension, not a sales gloss. B has useful bones, especially the FAA question, but "Consumer-Market Exit Two Years Ago Is Starting to Look Like the Right Call" declares victory before the facts can carry it. The difference is discipline: A asks for proof before it sells the angle; B keeps decorating gaps as conclusions.
gaps_in_A: "A US drone maker bets the grid will pay a premium to avoid Chinese hardware" overreaches on "pay a premium"; the update says US-made positioning against Chinese makers, not that utilities are paying more for it.
A treats the FAA/BVLOS issue as proof inside the operations angle, but misses it as a standalone aviation-regulation angle. B saw that lane more clearly.

"The launch is the first concrete evidence of where the 2024 exit led" is plausible, but not proven by the update; it says Skydio exited consumer drones two years ago, not that this is the first concrete post-exit evidence.
gaps_in_B: "trade policy created a buyer-side gap" is invented. The facts say Chinese drone makers face import restrictions; they do not establish a market gap or vacancy.
"starting to look like the right call" and "the first concrete evidence the bet is paying off" oversell the pivot. Unnamed utility contracts are not proof of strategic success.
"named (if unspecified) utility contracts" is sloppy and internally contradictory. They are not named, and "paying customers" goes beyond the supplied facts.

"a persistent monitoring layer with a different economics and reliability profile" decorates the product with unsupported economics and reliability claims. The release only gives docking, charging, scheduled flights, and automatic defect reports.
